Return order while you are saving: the same market factors can meet very different amounts of capital

Reverse a ten-year return sequence while keeping the contribution schedule unchanged, then compare portfolio value, contributed principal and modeled investment growth.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore ten return years while adding new savings

Interactive planning lab

Ending portfolio · reversed sequence, losses later$77,579.65
Initial capital plus deposits made in either path$70,000

Original deterministic ten-year total-return illustration. The annual return list is [-15%, -5%, 8%, 10%, 12%, 6%, 4%, 8%, 7%, 5%] times the selected scale. The second path reverses exactly those scaled returns. Both receive the same initial capital and equal deposits on the same eligible year-end dates. Each annual return applies before that year-end deposit; a deposit first earns return in the following year. The selected opening delay skips deposits without later catch-up. No contribution earns return before it arrives. All distributions are retained within the assumed total returns. There are no withdrawals, fees, taxes, market data, probabilities, investment recommendations or future-return estimates. The comparison keeps the same full-period product and arithmetic mean; with no deposits, the two ending values agree.

The central idea

When new money arrives during the path, the return on each contribution depends on which years remain. An unchanged full-period return product does not guarantee the same ending portfolio.

01

Hold the return set and saving schedule constant

The first scenario uses ten authored annual returns: negative 15%, negative 5%, then 8%, 10%, 12%, 6%, 4%, 8%, 7% and 5%. The second reverses exactly that list. Neither path is historical data or a forecast of an asset class.

Both start with CAD 10,000 and receive CAD 6,000 at each year-end in the default. The same contribution enters on the same date in both portfolios. Reversing the returns preserves their arithmetic mean and their full-period growth-factor product, allowing the comparison to focus on which return years occur after new capital arrives.

The scale control multiplies every return by the same selected percentage in both paths. It is another hypothetical stress, without a probability attached. It does not estimate volatility, change the amount saved or identify an investment capable of delivering the selected sequence.

02

Specify when a contribution begins earning return

Each year, the existing portfolio first receives that year’s total return. The deposit arrives afterward, at year-end. The new money therefore starts earning return in the following year. The final year-end deposit is included in ending wealth but earns no investment return inside the ten-year horizon.

For the early-loss path, CAD 10,000 falls to CAD 8,500 in year one, then receives the CAD 6,000 deposit and ends at CAD 14,500. The reversed path begins with a 5% return, reaches CAD 10,500 and then receives the same CAD 6,000, ending its first year at CAD 16,500.

Those first-year results do not settle the full comparison. Each later contribution encounters a different remaining set of returns in the two paths. A contribution made after the opening losses is not exposed to losses that occurred before it arrived.

03

Read the portfolio value beside the contribution ledger

The default initial amount and ten annual deposits sum to CAD 70,000 of contributed principal. The early-loss path finishes at approximately CAD 95,990.68. The reversed path, which puts the two negative returns at the end, finishes at approximately CAD 77,579.65.

Subtracting contributed principal gives approximately CAD 25,990.68 and CAD 7,579.65 of modeled investment growth. The signed comparison chart uses that difference rather than calling the entire account balance investment earnings. A larger balance can contain a large amount of the household’s own saving.

The endpoint difference is about CAD 18,411.02 despite the same ten return factors and contribution dates. It arises because a late return acts on capital that has accumulated from earlier deposits. This controlled example does not establish how much a real saver will gain or lose, or that future losses will occur at a convenient time.

04

Set contributions to zero to isolate the timing effect

With no new deposits, both scenarios end at the same value, apart from numerical rounding. The initial amount experiences every growth factor once. Changing their order does not change their product when there is no external cash flow.

With deposits, the initial capital still has the same full-period product in both cases, but each later deposit has its own shorter investment window. Its terminal value equals the contribution multiplied by only the growth factors that occur after it arrives. The portfolio endpoint is the sum of those separate amounts.

This also explains why increasing initial capital changes the account levels but does not change the contribution-driven endpoint difference under these particular fixed sequences. The initial-capital component is equal in both. Contributions and withdrawals can create return-order effects; their signs, dates and amounts determine the exposure rather than a single overall average.

05

Use the matrix without treating a saving delay as a recommendation

The matrix replaces the annual deposit and the number of opening years in which deposits are skipped. Each cell compares two portfolios with the same revised saving schedule. The total horizon remains ten years, and skipped contributions are not caught up later.

A positive cell means the early-loss sequence ends higher than its reverse under that cell’s assumptions. A zero cell can occur when there are no deposits or when the schedule leaves no meaningful return exposure after the final deposit. It is not evidence that saving less or waiting longer is a superior household strategy.

Comparisons across delay rows change how much principal is contributed as well as when it arrives. Read the principal total and the portfolio levels alongside any endpoint difference. The tool does not assign a probability to a market path, calculate the affordability of a contribution or determine whether a goal can tolerate a later start.

06

Connect contribution discipline with the time available for the goal

Investor.gov’s regular-investing explanation describes investing equal amounts at regular intervals. This example uses annual deposits to make timing visible; it does not calculate monthly share purchases or promise a profit from contributing through a decline.

For a real plan, record the contribution amount, arrival dates, intended use date and money that must remain accessible. A late loss can matter more when a large accumulated balance is close to being needed. The ability to continue saving and the flexibility of the goal are separate questions from the arithmetic of an average return.

The charts exclude fees, taxes, withdrawals and account contribution limits. All distributions remain inside the assumed total returns. Use the related retirement guide to examine withdrawals, where return order interacts with money leaving the portfolio. This article focuses on capital arriving over time and keeps that cash-flow assumption visible throughout the comparison.
